meta.tagline: Plan real travel in Shanghai & Zhejiang.
meta.contentNote: This demo contains draft, editorial content. Transport times, opening hours, ticket prices and entry rules change often and are marked “verify before travel” unless we state a checked date. Nothing on this site is a booking or a promise of service.

cities.name: Shanghai
cities.tagline: A global arrival point, and a city of layered neighborhoods worth slowing down for.
cities.intro: Most international visitors land here, and for good reason: Shanghai has the region's most complete travel infrastructure for non-Chinese speakers — metro signage in English throughout, easy airport links, and a dense core of walkable historic streets. It's also a very different city from the Jiangnan countryside an hour away. Use Shanghai for arrival, orientation and one or two unhurried neighborhood days, then point the second half of your trip toward Zhejiang.

facts.v: Two international airports (PVG and SHA) with metro links to the center. Rail hub at Hongqiao for Zhejiang connections.
Metro is extensive, cheap and signposted in English; ride-hailing apps are the easiest door-to-door option.
Mobile payment (Alipay / WeChat Pay) is dominant; international cards can be linked in recent versions.
1–3 days: one day of classic sights and one day of neighborhood walking, or a family day.
Spring and autumn are mildest. July–August is hot and humid.

cities.name: Hangzhou
cities.tagline: The classic Jiangnan city — best in the early morning, before the crowds wake up.
cities.intro: Hangzhou is the region's most famous postcard: West Lake, tea hills and temple lanes. It works well as a first Zhejiang stop after Shanghai — about an hour by high-speed rail. The honest advice: the lake rewards slow, early starts and walking rather than checklist sightseeing, and the city connects cleanly onward to Ningbo if you want to trade the famous scenery for a working port city with book culture and seafood.

facts.v: High-speed rail from Shanghai Hongqiao and connections from major hubs; East Railway Station is the main gateway.
Metro plus walking; the lake ring is best on foot or by bike share.
1–3 days: one slow lake day, one tea-and-temple day if time allows.
The lakefront is busiest 10:00–16:00 on weekends and holidays. Go early.
Spring (tea season) and autumn; summer is hot, winter can be misty and quiet.

cities.name: Ningbo
cities.tagline: A working harbor city of books, seafood and old streets — our first pilot city.
cities.intro: Ningbo is our early pilot city. It is not a lakes-and-pagodas postcard like Hangzhou; it is a real, working port — China's oldest surviving private library (Tianyi Pavilion, founded 1561), early treaty-port streets along the old Bund, a deep seafood tradition, and easy access toward Buddhist temples and the Putuoshan ferry route. We are testing whether a well-explained Ningbo story earns two extra days from visitors who land in Shanghai or Hangzhou. That is an assumption to validate, not a proven demand — but the material is strong.

facts.v: High-speed rail from Shanghai Hongqiao (around 2 hours) and from Hangzhou East (around 1 hour).
Metro lines plus walking for the historic core; taxis or ride-hailing for Dongqian Lake and the temples.
2 days: one day of Tianyi Pavilion, Moon Lake, the old Bund and seafood; one day at Dongqian Lake or the Zen temples.
The Putuoshan ferry route runs from nearby ports (e.g., Zhujiajian); sailings depend on weather.
Spring and autumn; seafood is best in autumn and winter months.

cities.name: Shaoxing
cities.tagline: Canals, yellow-wine culture and a quieter old town — a preview, not yet a guide.
cities.intro: Shaoxing is on our shortlist for future coverage: water-town streets, wine-cellars that produce Shaoxing rice wine, and a strong literary heritage. We are still gathering and verifying local detail, so for now this is a preview only — no routes, timetables or prices are published here.

cities.name: Zhoushan
cities.tagline: Islands and the ferry route to Putuoshan — a preview, not yet a guide.
cities.intro: Zhoushan is the island prefecture that includes the Putuoshan ferry gateway. It matters for our Buddhist-route logic (see the Ningbo temples route), but we have not yet verified ferry schedules, seasons or island logistics to a standard we would publish. Preview only for now.

routes.title: Ningbo in Two Days: Port, Books & Seafood
routes.summary: Two honest days in a working port city: China's oldest surviving private library, a treaty-port waterfront, lake-and-temple quiet, and seafood at every meal. Draft route — not field-verified.
routes.why: Shanghai and Hangzhou are the familiar gateways. Ningbo shows a different Zhejiang: less lakeside scenery, more harbor, streets, libraries and meals. It is two hours by rail from Shanghai and one from Hangzhou — close enough to be a considered add-on, far enough to feel like a real second destination.

routes.title: Buddhist Zhejiang: Temples & the Road to Putuoshan
routes.summary: Tiantong and Asoka temples from a Ningbo base, with the logic for continuing toward Putuoshan by ferry — a route that depends heavily on weather and schedules. Draft, not verified.
routes.why: Eastern Zhejiang is one of China's densest Buddhist regions. Ningbo's temples are accessible, quieter than Hangzhou's famous monastery, and the natural first stop on the way to Putuoshan, one of China's four sacred Buddhist mountains.

routes.title: From Shanghai: Add a Port City (2 Days)

routes.why: Two hours on the train buys you a genuinely different Zhejiang: a working harbor, a 450-year-old library, and seafood. It is the cheapest 'second destination' available from Shanghai, but it is not for everyone — this route explains the trade-off honestly.

faqs.q: How do I get from Shanghai to Ningbo?
faqs.a: High-speed rail from Shanghai Hongqiao takes roughly 2 hours; from Hangzhou East it's roughly 1 hour. Times and stations change, so verify the schedule for your date before booking — this is a demo seed answer, not a live timetable.

faqs.q: Can I pay with my international card in China?
faqs.a: Mobile payment is dominant. Recent versions of Alipay and WeChat Pay allow linking international cards, which is the most practical route for tourists; card acceptance at physical shops varies. Set this up and test it before you travel, and carry some cash as backup. Verify current rules — payment policies change.

faqs.q: How do I stay connected / get data?
faqs.a: Most international travelers use a travel eSIM or a roaming plan before arrival. Note that many foreign apps and services behave differently on Chinese networks. Arranging connectivity in advance is the common approach — verify your provider's current China coverage.

faqs.q: How do I book high-speed train tickets?
faqs.a: Tickets can be bought on the official railway app (12306) and at station counters with a passport. Booking ahead is wise on weekends and holidays. Counter queues can be long, so the app with an English-friendly payment setup is usually easier. Verify current booking rules.

faqs.q: Are there luggage lockers at train stations?
faqs.a: Major stations generally offer luggage storage services, sometimes staffed counters rather than coin lockers. Sizes, prices and hours vary by station — check on arrival, and keep valuables with you.

It depends on what you want. Ningbo offers a working port city with Tianyi Pavilion (a library from 1561), a treaty-port riverside, and serious seafood — a different Zhejiang from Hangzhou's lake scenery. If your priority is postcard landscapes, stay at the lake. We're testing this question ourselves; treat our recommendation as an assumption, not a proven fact.

faqs.q: What should I eat in Ningbo?
faqs.a: The signatures: tangyuan (sweet glutinous rice balls, the city's most famous dish), fresh seafood (best in autumn and winter months), and preserved-vegetable dishes. Nantang Old Street is the easiest place to try several staples in one walk; for seafood, ask for the day's catch.

faqs.q: Is Dongqian Lake a good day trip?
faqs.a: For a scenery day without leaving Ningbo, yes — cycle paths, boats and lakeside tea houses. Bike rental points and boat docks change; verify on site. Give it a half to full day.

faqs.q: How do I get to Putuoshan?
faqs.a: Ferries to Putuoshan run from nearby ports such as Zhujiajian; sailings depend on weather and season. Plan flexibly, verify the schedule for your dates, and book island accommodation if staying. See our Buddhist Zhejiang route for the full logic.

faqs.q: What should I know before visiting temples?
faqs.a: Dress modestly (shoulders and knees covered), keep voices low, and don't photograph inside halls where signs prohibit it. Hours and entrance fees vary; check before going. Tiantong and Asoka temples near Ningbo are quieter than Hangzhou's Lingyin but just as meaningful.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit?
faqs.a: Spring (tea season, mild) and autumn (seafood season, clear skies) are the most comfortable. July–August is hot and humid; winter is cold and can be misty — atmospheric at the lake, hard on long walking days.
Tipping is not expected in China. Service charges, where they exist, are added to the bill. Just pay the bill.

faqs.q: How do I handle the language barrier?
faqs.a: Metro and major sights are signposted in English; small restaurants and taxis often aren't. A translation app on your phone, plus showing destination names in Chinese characters (we include them in our guides), sorts out most situations. If you're stuck, ask the assistant here for phrasing — or use the consult form and a real person will help you sort it out.
Police 110, ambulance 120, fire 119. If you're unsure about anything medical, legal or visa-related, seek official sources or local help — we cannot make those judgments for you.

Visa and entry rules depend on your nationality and current policy — they change and we cannot judge your personal eligibility. Check your country's Chinese embassy or consulate website and official announcements for the rules that apply to you. This site does not replace official immigration information.

faqs.q: Can you book hotels, trains or tours for me?
faqs.a: No — this demo does not sell or book anything. We give you route logic, transport notes and what to verify. For bookings, use official channels (railway app, hotels directly). If you'd like human help planning, use the consult form — a real person will follow up, and we never promise unverified prices or availability.

steps.title: Choose English on the home screen
steps.detail: Most machines show a language button, usually a flag icon or the word English, in a corner of the screen.
steps.tip: If the screen is already in English, skip this step.

steps.title: Select your destination line or station
steps.detail: Metro systems in Shanghai, Hangzhou and Ningbo sell tickets by destination station. Tap the line, then the station name.
steps.tip: Your destination names in Chinese are included in our city guides — show them to a staff member if needed.

steps.title: Pay at the machine
steps.detail: Machines accept cash and mobile payment. International card acceptance varies by machine and city.
steps.tip: Carry small banknotes as backup.

steps.title: Take your ticket and change
steps.detail: Collect the ticket and any coins from the tray. Your ticket is used at both entry and exit gates.
steps.tip: Keep it — you need it to exit.

photoGuides.verifyNote: Machine interfaces and payment methods differ by city and station. This is a simulated demo tutorial.

photoGuides.scenario: Storing bags at a train station

steps.title: Look for a staffed counter or locker bank
steps.detail: Major stations often have staffed luggage storage rather than coin lockers. Follow luggage or baggage symbols.
steps.tip: Allow extra time before a train if you plan to store bags.

steps.title: Show your passport and ticket
steps.detail: Staffed counters typically record your ID and a fee is charged by item and size.
steps.tip: Have small cash or a working mobile payment ready.

steps.title: Photograph your receipt or token
steps.detail: If you receive a numbered tag or receipt, photograph it in case it is lost.
steps.tip: This also helps staff help you later.

steps.title: Note the closing time
steps.detail: Storage counters close, often earlier than the station. Collect bags before the stated time.
steps.tip: Ask the closing time in writing or on screen before you leave.

photoGuides.verifyNote: Storage availability varies by station. This is a simulated demo tutorial.

photoGuides.scenario: Ordering at a fast-food or casual restaurant

steps.title: Check for an English option
steps.detail: Many chain kiosks have a language switch. If none, use a translation app's camera mode on the screen.
steps.tip: Chains are the most predictable place to practice.

steps.title: Order by category
steps.detail: Menus are usually organized by category: mains, drinks, desserts. Tap an item, then a size or quantity.
steps.tip: Photos on the screen are your best guide.

steps.title: Review the order screen
steps.detail: Confirm items and quantities before paying. A red button usually confirms; verify the total.
steps.tip: If something looks wrong, tap back or ask staff.

steps.title: Pay and take the receipt
steps.detail: Pay by mobile or cash per the machine; take the numbered receipt and wait for your number.
steps.tip: The receipt number is shown on a screen when your order is ready.

photoGuides.verifyNote: Interfaces vary by brand. This is a simulated demo tutorial.

photoGuides.scenario: Reading a seafood or local menu

steps.title: Photograph the menu with a translation app
steps.detail: Camera translation handles printed menus well. Check the dish before ordering if you have allergies.
steps.tip: Screenshots or photos work offline in some apps.

steps.title: Identify the sections
steps.detail: Look for headings: seafood, vegetables, soup, rice/noodles. Our Ningbo food notes tell you what to look for.
steps.tip: Seafood menus often list 'market price' — ask the price before confirming.

steps.title: Order the day's catch
steps.detail: For seafood, the day's catch is usually the best and often cheapest. Ask for a recommendation.
steps.tip: Point at the item and show the Chinese name from our guide.

steps.title: Confirm price and quantity
steps.detail: Seafood is often priced by weight. Agree the price and weight before it is cooked.
steps.tip: This is normal practice, not a negotiation tactic — but always confirm first.

photoGuides.verifyNote: This guide is the lowest-confidence demo: menus vary completely by restaurant. When unsure, ask staff or switch to the kiosk/consult paths.

photoGuides.scenario: Reading signs at a metro or rail station

steps.title: Follow the line color, not just the name
steps.detail: Metro lines have distinct colors and numbers; signs show both. Match color + number to your route.
steps.tip: Our city guides list the lines for key places.

steps.title: Look for exit letters or numbers
steps.detail: Stations label exits with letters or numbers. The exit matters — check which one your destination needs.

assumptions.s: Assumption — to be validated by usage behavior, not signups.

assumptions.a: Travelers will trust visibly-flagged 'verify before travel' content
assumptions.s: Assumption — trust signals are a hypothesis too.

assumptions.a: Users want to save routes into a simple trip list

assumptions.a: Human consult should be low-pressure and gradual
assumptions.s: Design principle — to be checked against consult form drop-off.
